articles.title: Martin Margiela's first portfolio for his future fashion house was stolen on a train; 39 years later, it sold for €24,700
articles.summary: A portfolio Martin Margiela created in 1987 while developing the idea for his future fashion house was stolen on a train and recovered by police a year
articles.body: A portfolio Martin Margiela created in 1987 while developing the idea for his future fashion house was stolen on a train and recovered by police a year later. Nearly four decades later, the portfolio was offered at auction in Paris in July, as part of a sale drawn from Margiela's personal archives. Described by Maurice Auction as the first portfolio illustrating the future Maison Martin Margiela, the 1987 dossier contains 13 A3-format pages of drawings, facsimiles and collages setting out the aesthetic of the then-unnamed house. Estimated at €5,000 to €8,000, it sold for €24,700 at the July 9, 2026 sale, including fees. The archive sale also brought together sketches, prototypes, garments and personal objects spanning Margiela’s career and later years at Hermès.Martin Margiela's 1987 portfolio captured the idea behind his future fashion houseThe portfolio dates to the period before Maison Martin Margiela was established in 1988. In his note accompanying the auction lot, Margiela recalled that he was looking for a manufacturer in Italy and needed to visualise the fashion he wanted to create. He drew silhouettes and accessories for his imagined fashion house and assembled them in a white cotton-covered folder. Maurice Auction describes the resulting dossier as the first portfolio illustrating the future Maison Martin Margiela and says its 13 A3-format pages of drawings, facsimiles and collages set out the house's aesthetic.The folder was later stolen on a train. Margiela made another version for his travels, using photocopies of the drawings. He recalled that he considered the photocopies more contemporary than the original pencil sketches and was able to create an almost identical portfolio. A year later, police recovered the stolen folder, after which Margiela compared the two versions and was struck by their similarity. The auction catalogue gives the provenance of the portfolio offered for sale as Margiela's personal archives, but does not specify whether the lot was the recovered original or the replacement.The archive sale traced Margiela's career from 1984 onwardsThe 1987 portfolio was part of a wider sale of Margiela's personal archives organised by Maurice Auction in collaboration with Kerry Taylor Auctions. The auction house said the material covered the period from 1984 to 2008 and included photographs, drawings and objects, alongside some pieces made during the pandemic. The sale brought together material from different stages of Margiela's career, including work from before the creation of his own fashion house.Among the earliest material were pieces associated with the Golden Spindle competition in Antwerp. Maurice Auction's English catalogue uses “Golden Spindle” as the translation of the French Canette d'Or. The archive included sketches, prototypes and presentation material connected with this early period. The auction also included a fashion drawing from Paris dated 1985. Estimated at €1,500 to €2,000, the drawing sold for €18,200. The archive extended into Margiela's later career and his period at Hermès, where he was responsible for the women's collections from 1997 to 2003. Among the personal objects offered was a white cotton working blouse from Margiela's personal archives, catalogued as dating from 1988–2008. The auction catalogue says the blouse was signed ‘Martin’ by the designer and bears substantial paint marks consistent with its use as workwear. Estimated at €6,000 to €10,000, it sold for €41,600.The graffiti Tabi boots became the sale's top resultAnother major lot was a pair of white-painted Tabi ankle boots associated with the 1991 Palais Galliera exhibition The World According to Its Creators. The exhibition invited visitors to write messages on its white-painted walls and floor. According to Margiela's account in the auction catalogue, visitors also unexpectedly wrote on the white-painted Tabi boots, leaving them covered in graffiti. This makes it more accurate to say that the boots were displayed at the exhibition and subsequently covered with writing by visitors, rather than describing the graffiti as something specifically created for the exhibition.Estimated at €30,000 to €50,000, the Tabi boots achieved a result of €364,000 including fees. Maurice Auction's sale information states that buyer fees were 25% excluding tax, or 30% including tax. On that basis, the corresponding hammer price would be approximately €280,000, although that figure is a calculation rather than the auction house's published result. The sale also included later pieces in which Margiela revisited his earlier work. Lot 46 was a one-of-a-kind sweater made from grey cotton socks, inspired by his Autumn-Winter 1991–1992 collection and created by the designer around 2020. Estimated at €25,000 to €40,000, it sold for €117,000. Unlike an earlier description of the piece, it was not a miniature reconstruction.The 1987 dossier offers a glimpse of Margiela before the label existedThe value of the archive lies not only in the prices achieved at auction but also in the way its contents document Margiela's working process. The material spans sketches, photographs, prototypes, garments, personal objects and documents from before and during the years of Maison Martin Margiela. The 1987 portfolio is particularly revealing because it predates the official establishment of the fashion house. Its drawings and collages show Margiela working out the visual identity of a fashion label that, at the time, existed only as an idea. The story behind the folder adds another layer to that history: it was stolen on a train, prompted Margiela to make an almost identical replacement, and was recovered by police a year later. Decades afterward, material from that formative period was released from his personal archives and offered to collectors and institutions.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A pair of gold Jordans was donated to an Oregon shelter; later found to be custom-made for Spike Lee, they sold for $50,800
articles.summary: A pair of striking gold Nike Air Jordan 3 sneakers ended up in a donation bin at the Portland Rescue Mission in Oregon in 2023, where staff initially
articles.body: A pair of striking gold Nike Air Jordan 3 sneakers ended up in a donation bin at the Portland Rescue Mission in Oregon in 2023, where staff initially suspected they were counterfeit. The shoes had been anonymously donated and were discovered by James Free, a man participating in the shelter's long-term programme, while he was sorting through donated items. Their unusual appearance eventually prompted staff to seek expert authentication. The sneakers turned out to be part of a tiny batch of custom Air Jordan 3s created by Nike designer Tinker Hatfield for filmmaker Spike Lee and people in his inner circle. After being authenticated, the rare shoes were put up for auction by Sotheby's and sold for $50,800 in December 2023.Rare Spike Lee Jordans discovered in donation binThe sneakers were placed in a donation chute at the Portland Rescue Mission's Burnside Shelter in April 2023. They eventually made their way into a basement donation bin containing clothing, blankets, coats, sleeping bags and shoes.James Free, who was living in the Mission's long-term shelter programme at the time, spotted the bright gold sneakers near the bottom of the bin. Their appearance immediately caught his attention, and he brought them to Erin Holcomb, the organisation's director of staff ministry.The shoes were in remarkably good condition. However, the circumstances surrounding their discovery made the staff suspicious. Holcomb initially believed they were likely high-quality fakes and did not immediately realise that the shelter had received an extremely rare pair of sneakers.Why the shoes were linked to Spike LeeThe sneakers were custom-made in 2019 by Nike footwear designer Tinker Hatfield for Spike Lee and members of his inner circle.Lee wore his own pair of the gold Air Jordan 3s at the 2019 Academy Awards. He wore them while attending the ceremony and later while accepting the Oscar for best adapted screenplay for BlacKkKlansman.The Portland pair was not Lee's personal pair. The donated sneakers were size 12½, while Lee has said that he wears a size 9½. They were part of a very limited run, with the Portland Rescue Mission describing them as one of only four or five pairs made for Lee's inner circle.The shoes also carried distinctive details connected to Lee. One heel featured the Jumpman logo, while the other carried the logo of his production company, 40 Acres and a Mule Filmworks. The gold colour and customised design made them unlike ordinary retail Air Jordan releases.Staff initially thought they were fakeHolcomb kept the sneakers for several weeks before taking them to Index, a sneaker consignment shop in Portland, to determine whether they were genuine.According to Holcomb's account, she approached the shop expecting an expert to confirm her suspicion that the shoes were counterfeit. Instead, the inspection produced a very different answer.Terrance Ricketts, co-owner of the store, determined that the shoes were authentic. He recognised their unusual construction, materials and markings and told Holcomb that Nike had produced only a handful of them. He estimated that they could be worth between $15,000 and $20,000.That discovery changed the Mission's plans for the shoes. Rather than distributing them as ordinary donated footwear, staff began looking for a way to authenticate and sell them while directing the proceeds towards the organisation's work.Tinker Hatfield authenticated the sneakersThe Mission then contacted Sotheby's, the international auction house, which agreed to handle the sale.Hatfield, who had designed the sneakers, also became involved. He authenticated the shoes and provided additional items for the auction, including a replacement box and an original design concept board. He also visited the Portland Rescue Mission and signed the materials connected to the sneakers.Sotheby's listed the sneakers with an estimated value of $15,000 to $20,000. The auction house also waived its seller's fee, allowing the proceeds from the sale to benefit the Portland Rescue Mission.The identity of the person who originally donated the shoes remained unknown. Even Lee said he did not know how the size 12½ pair had ended up in the shelter's donation system.The auction ends at $50,800The auction produced a much higher result than the initial estimate.As the Sotheby's auction approached its conclusion in December 2023, staff at the Portland Rescue Mission gathered to watch the bidding. The amount eventually climbed sharply during the final minutes.The winning bid reached $50,800, more than twice Sotheby's initial high estimate of $20,000. Staff members at the Mission watched the final moments together and celebrated when the auction closed.The Portland Rescue Mission said the money would support its work helping people experiencing homelessness, including providing shelter, meals, clothing and other services.From a donation bin to a $50,800 auctionWhat made the discovery unusual was the chain of events behind it. A pair of highly limited sneakers connected to one of Hollywood's best-known filmmakers had been anonymously donated to a homeless shelter and ended up buried beneath ordinary donated goods.The shoes were initially mistaken for fakes, then identified by a sneaker expert, authenticated by their original designer and ultimately sold at a major international auction house.The original donor was never identified, but the unexpected donation generated $50,800 for the Portland Rescue Mission, turning an overlooked pair of sneakers at the bottom of a donation bin into a substantial source of funding for the shelter.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2001, the Indian Mesa wind farm began operating in Pecos County with 125 turbines; sheep grazing continued, and $930,000 was paid in school taxes
articles.summary: In May 2001, the Indian Mesa wind farm began operating in Pecos County, West Texas, with 125 turbines and a total installed capacity of 82.5 MW.
articles.body: In May 2001, the Indian Mesa wind farm began operating in Pecos County, West Texas, with 125 turbines and a total installed capacity of 82.5 MW. The project sits on a mesa where the uses of the land include grazing livestock, primarily sheep, and hunting, and the project does not limit these uses. According to the US Government Accountability Office (GAO), the project paid about $930,000 in local school district taxes in 2003. The details appear in report GAO-04-756, published in September 2004, which summarises visits to nine wind power projects in five states.When did the Indian Mesa wind farm in Texas begin operatingThe Indian Mesa project is in Pecos County, Texas, and is owned by FPL Energy, a company based in Florida. The report states that the project started operating in May 2001 and has 125 turbines, with a total installed capacity of 82.5 MW. The GAO lists the power purchasers as the Lower Colorado River Authority and Texas Utilities Company, and records four landowners.The GAO states that "the Indian Mesa wind farm is located in West Texas, an area with strong, sustained wind resources." The report gives an annual generation estimate of 250 million kWh for the project. In its wider findings, the GAO notes that California and Texas accounted for about one-half of the nation's 6,374 MW of installed wind generation capacity at the end of 2003, and its state-by-state figure for Texas is 1,293.0 MW.How much land does the Indian Mesa wind farm occupyThe GAO reports that "the project is located on 34,000 acres situated on a mesa" and that "one of the four landowners of this acreage is the University of Texas." According to the report, "about 7,000 of these acres are leased for the project." It continues: "The uses of the land include grazing livestock, primarily sheep and hunting. The project does not limit these uses."On the wider question of land use, the GAO's introductory letter states that "even large wind turbines use only about a quarter-acre of land each, including access roads, so farmers can continue to plant crops and graze livestock up to the base of the turbines." The report also records that "University of Texas officials indicated that legal and technical resources available to the university were critical to negotiating a favourable lease agreement for a wind project on university property." In its general description of how wind projects are developed, the GAO lists a lease or easement agreement with a term "sufficient for financing the project, usually 25 years or more."How did the project support local training through its tax agreementAccording to the GAO, "as an incentive for locating the project in Pecos County, the county provided the project with a full property tax abatement for 5 years." The report adds that "in return, the project owner (at that time) agreed to donate funds in an amount equivalent to about 10 per cent of the abated taxes to a regional technical training centre." The GAO also states that "the owner also agreed to hire and use local companies and labour for the construction of the project, to the extent possible."The report then records that "the project paid about $930,000 in local school district taxes in 2003." A footnote in the report explains that "because one of the four landowners was a county commissioner, property taxes were assessed for this landowner's parcel to avoid the appearance of a conflict of interest." The GAO does not specify which school districts received the payment in its account of Indian Mesa.How did wind power projects affect Pecos County school tax revenuesAccording to the GAO, "in Pecos County, Texas, with a population of about 16,000 the school districts received about $5 million in 2002 from property tax revenues directly associated with wind power projects in that county." The report states that "the Iraan-Sheffield School District, obtained one-third of its property tax revenues from wind power projects that year" and that "these projects also added about 30 to 35 full-time permanent jobs to operate and maintain the projects." It also cites the Fort Stockton Economic Development Corporation, which said "the county experienced a 10 percent increase in gross sales during the construction of several wind power projects."On employment at Indian Mesa itself, the GAO states that "the project owner currently employs 43 people to operate and maintain the four wind projects the company owns in the area, including the Indian Mesa project." The report continues: "In the future, the owner plans to hire 4 additional people after the warranty and maintenance agreement with the turbine manufacturer expires." Separately, the GAO asked the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) to model hypothetical projects. The GAO asked NREL to model hypothetical scenarios. In one, building a 150 MW project owned by an out-of-area company in Pecos County would create "the equivalent of only 36 full-time jobs for 1 year in the county". That project is nearly twice Indian Mesa's 82.5 MW, and the GAO said it did not expect high accuracy from the model.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 237 vehicles fined for illegal parking on NH in Dhanbad
articles.summary: Dhanbad NH task force fined 237 vehicles Rs 21.5 lakh for illegal roadside parking since Sept 26, launching ongoing enforcement after fatal Sept 24 crash.
articles.body: Dhanbad: The National Highway Task Force has intensified its crackdown on vehicles parked illegally along national highways, collecting around Rs 21.5 lakh in fines from 237 vehicles during a special enforcement drive since Sept 26, officials said on Thursday.The campaign was launched to ensure smooth and safe traffic movement and prevent accidents caused by vehicles parked along busy highway stretches.Officials said several heavy and commercial vehicles were found parked haphazardly on the roadside in violation of traffic regulations, posing a serious risk to motorists.The enforcement drive was conducted jointly by the district transport officer, motor vehicle inspector, district road safety team, police officials and the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) route patrolling vehicle team. The vehicles found violating parking rules were penalised under provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act.Dhanbad DC Aditya Ranjan said the administration was taking the issue of road safety seriously and that the enforcement campaign would continue. He said strict action would be taken against motorists violating traffic regulations.Along with issuing challans, the task force conducted a road safety awareness campaign among drivers and the general public. Drivers were instructed not to park vehicles illegally on national highways or along their edges and to use designated parking areas.Officials said roadside parking, particularly by heavy vehicles, can obstruct traffic movement and reduce visibility for approaching motorists, increasing the possibility of serious accidents.The crackdown has gained significance following the Sept 24 accident in which four children, including Trisha Singh, daughter of rural development minister Deepika Pandey Singh, were killed after their car rammed into a truck parked on the roadside. articles.title: PU marks 109 years without Foundation Day celebrations
articles.summary: Patna University enters 110th year as foundation day events are skipped; officials cite VC’s chancellor meeting, with celebrations to be held later.
articles.body: Patna: A university that once shaped the intellectual, academic and political life of Bihar crossed a historic milestone on Thursday—but without the ceremony that normally marks such an occasion.Patna University (PU), the seventh-oldest university in the Indian subcontinent and Bihar’s first, completed 109 years and entered its 110th year on Oct 1. Yet the campus remained without the foundation day lecture, ceremonial function, gold medal distribution for toppers, or other traditional events associated with the occasion.A senior PU official told TOI that Thursday’s programme could not be held because vice-chancellor Ajay Kumar Singh was scheduled to attend a meeting convened by the chancellor at Lok Bhawan. The official said the celebrations would be held later.The low-key observance drew disappointment from alumni, teachers, students and non-teaching staff, who said the foundation day is a key occasion to reconnect the university community with PU’s history and academic traditions.Former dean of social sciences Nawal Kishore Chaudhary criticised what he called an apathetic approach by the authorities. “The foundation day should be celebrated on the scheduled date,” he said.The absence of celebrations was noted more sharply in light of past practice, when foundation day functions routinely included formal lectures by eminent guests and felicitation of undergraduate toppers with gold medals.The university also did not hold a Teachers’ Day programme on Sept 5 this year, which had previously been observed annually.Established by the Patna University Act, which came into force on Oct 1, 1917, the university initially served as an affiliating and examining authority over a vast educational territory covering Bihar, Odisha and Nepal. articles.summary: Ranchi administration directs GAIL to restore roads damaged by gas pipeline work, fill pits, add barricading, follow safety norms, and coordinate with NHAI/RCD.
articles.body: Ranchi: The district administration has directed GAIL and its contractors to restore roads damaged during the ongoing gas pipeline works and ensure adequate safety measures at construction sites to prevent inconvenience to commuters.Sadar sub-divisional officer Kumar Rajat, in a meeting with GAIL officials and contractors on Thursday, reviewed the progress of pipeline and road works, restoration of damaged stretches, safety arrangements and adherence to project timelines and issued the directions.Taking cognisance of road damage at several locations due to ongoing pipeline work, DC Manjunath Bhajantri directed GAIL and its contractors to take corrective measures on priority and restore affected roads to their original condition after completion of the work.During the review meeting, Rajat directed contractors to immediately fill pits dug during construction or pipeline laying and ensure that the roads are levelled and made fit for traffic once the work is completed. He stressed that commuters should not be forced to face prolonged inconvenience because of unfinished restoration work.The SDO also instructed contractors to put in place proper barricading and other safety arrangements throughout the duration of the work. Work sites must have measures to facilitate the safe movement of vehicles and pedestrians and prevent accidents, officials said.“Construction and pipeline work should not leave roads in a condition that causes prolonged inconvenience to the public,” Rajat said.He added that contractors would be responsible for the quality of restoration and ensuring that affected roads are traffic-worthy after completion.GAIL officials were also asked to coordinate with National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) and Road Construction Department (RCD) to ensure timely execution of projects and better coordination among agencies.Rajat directed officials and contractors to complete the projects within the stipulated timeframe and regularly monitor the progress of work. articles.summary: A North Carolina family has conserved 298 acres of their land, preserving its historical and environmental significance for future generations. This conservation easement ensures the land remains undeveloped after seven generations of stewardship by the Caldwell-Dietzel family.
articles.body: A North Carolina family has held on to part of the same property for seven generations, more than 200 years after its ancestors bought the land. Now, 298 acres of that historic holding have been placed under permanent conservation protection.The land in Robeson County was purchased by John W. Caldwell and his wife, Nancy Hartfield, in 1811. They had moved from Kinston, North Carolina, to the Raft Swamp area near Lumberton before acquiring the 600-acre property.Last year, on June 9, Three Rivers Land Trust, a non-profit conservation organisation, protected 298 acres of land through a conservation easement, ensuring the property cannot be developed into housing or used for commercial purposes, according to the trust.The agreement covers most of the land that remains with the family today. Of the original 600 acres, 306 acres are still family-owned, with Joe and Rosalie Dietzel and their son, Charles Dietzel, now responsible for its stewardship.The conservation deal means the protected acreage will remain undeveloped rather than being converted into a residential neighbourhood, covered with houses and asphalt or turned into a commercial site.Land passed down through seven generationsThe property has remained connected to the Caldwell-Dietzel family for 214 years, although the way the land has been used has changed over time.More than 200 acres of the property were once cultivated for tobacco. The land is now covered by longleaf and loblolly pine trees and is managed as working forestland.For the family, preserving the property is not only about maintaining the forest. Keeping the land within the family has been one of its key goals.Joe Dietzel said the family wanted to continue the agricultural legacy established by John Caldwell and Nancy Hartfield and eventually pass it to future descendants.“We are deeply honoured and humbled to be able to continue the agricultural legacy of John and Nancy and to pass that legacy on to our descendants,” Dietzel said.The conservation easement gives that intention a permanent legal framework for the 298 acres.While the family retains ownership, the agreement restricts future development of the protected land. It will continue to be used as forestland rather than being opened up for residential or commercial construction.From tobacco farming to pine treesThe landscape has changed significantly since the property was first acquired.Tobacco was once a major part of the family’s use of the land, with more than 200 acres devoted to the crop. Today, longleaf and loblolly pines dominate the property.The family’s management of the forest has also brought recognition from organisations involved in forestry and conservation.The North Carolina Forest Service has recognised the landowners for their efforts to care for the property.The family also became the first landowners from Robeson County to be included in the Longleaf Alliance’s “Longleaf Honour Roll”.That recognition came as the family continued managing the forest while retaining its connection to the property across generations.“The Dietzel family are remarkable stewards of their land and are deeply committed to its permanent conservation,” Emily Callicutt, director of conservation at Three Rivers Land Trust, said.298 acres protected from future developmentThe agreement does not transfer the land to the land trust. Instead, the conservation easement places permanent restrictions on how the 298 acres can be developed.That distinction allows the family to continue owning the property while preventing future development that could fundamentally change its use.The protected acreage will not become a housing development or commercial property. The land will remain undeveloped and continue to showcase the family’s longstanding connection to agriculture and forestry.The agreement also reflects a wider effort by Three Rivers Land Trust to protect family-owned agricultural land.“Saving family farms is one of our core missions,” Travis Morehead, executive director of Three Rivers Land Trust, said. “We understand the significance of agriculture in North Carolina and are proud to help this family conserve their land.”A 214-year connection continuesThe conservation agreement comes more than two centuries after the original 600-acre purchase.Only part of that original holding remains with the family today, but the 306 acres that survived seven generations are still under family stewardship.Of that remaining property, 298 acres are now protected from future development.For the Caldwell-Dietzel family, the deal puts a permanent safeguard around a piece of land that has outlasted generations of owners, changes in agriculture and the transition from tobacco cultivation to managed pine forest.You use AI every day. articles.title: Latest taxpayer-funded ad promotes Trump war with Iran
articles.summary: The Trump administration is airing another taxpayer-funded ad, this time touting the seven-month Iran war. In the commercial, which ad-tracking firm Medium Buying shared Wednesday on social media, audio of President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth plays in the background as U.S. military footage — including unclassified strikes — is displayed. “This regime will…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is airing another taxpayer-funded ad , this time touting the seven-month Iran war .

In the commercial, which ad-tracking firm Medium Buying shared Wednesday on social media, audio of President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth plays in the background as U.S. military footage — including unclassified strikes — is displayed.

“This regime will soon learn that no one should challenge the strength and might of the United States,” Trump remarked, referring to the Islamic Republic.

“If you kill Americans, if you threaten Americans anywhere on Earth, we will hunt you down without apology and without hesitation and we will kill you,” Hegseth said in the ad.

The Defense secretary added, “We didn’t start this war, but under President Trump, we are finishing it.”

The ad closes with the president saying, in the early days of the war, the Iranian people should “take over their government” when the U.S. concludes its military operation.

The Iran war, which Trump initially said would last roughly a month, hit the seven-month mark this week without any public sign of a lasting deal to end hostilities. Nearly two-thirds of respondents to a recent CNN/SSRS poll said the U.S. is not winning the conflict.

The ad includes a disclaimer that reads, “Paid for by the U.S. government,” making it one of multiple taxpayer-funded commercials the administration has aired in recent weeks.

One ad features Trump saying, “Together we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America,” as the song “Love Me” by JMSN, whose name is Christian Berishaj, plays in the background.

The administration has reportedly diverted funding for the Department of Homeland Security to pay for the ads, which Senate Democrats rang alarm bells over on Wednesday.

Public officials cannot use taxpayer dollars for campaign purposes, as stipulated by the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971 .

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said Monday the anti-communism message in one of the ads was “great,” but it should not be paid for using taxpayer dollars.

The White House has defended the clips, arguing in a Friday release they are “clearly not campaign ads” because the president is not on the ballot in November. Trump has instructed voters to “pretend” as if he were on the ballot in the midterms.

“Instead, the announcements are a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending — at home, at the border, and abroad,” the White House added. “That’s not partisanship — that’s a government that still believes in the country it serves.”

Trump also said Wednesday the ads are “for the spirit of the country” and do not promote a candidate.

“These are ads for the country. … I’m not promoting myself because I’m not running for office. I’m promoting the country,” he told reporters in the Oval Office.

articles.title: Motionless bodies, desperate hands: Heartbreaking scenes at Diveagar beach as locals fight to save Pune students; what we know
articles.summary: RAIGAD: It was a heartbreaking scene at Maharashtra’s Diveagar beach on Thursday.
articles.body: RAIGAD: It was a heartbreaking scene at Maharashtra’s Diveagar beach on Thursday.Young students lay motionless on the shore as locals and rescuers desperately tried to bring them back to life. Some were seen administering CPR, while others frantically rubbed the children's feet and tried every possible way to revive them.The shoreline echoed with frantic cries and the blaring of ambulances as desperate efforts continued to save the young lives.The beach, which had welcomed a group of students from Pune for a picnic, had suddenly turned into a scene of unimaginable grief. Those present watched helplessly as rescuers battled against time, hoping for a miracle.But the desperate efforts could not undo the tragedy. Eight students from a private coaching institute in Alandi, Pune, drowned after being swept away by strong currents at Diveagar beach. All eight bodies were eventually recovered, police said.What happened at Diveagar Beach?According to a police official, a group of 48 people, comprising 25 boys, 17 girls and six teachers, had travelled to Diveagar for a picnic. The beach falls under the jurisdiction of Dighi coastal police station.Eight students ventured into the sea but were swept away after misjudging the depth of the water and the strength of the current, the official said.All 8 bodies recoveredSearch and rescue teams rushed to the beach after receiving an alert and recovered all eight bodies. The deceased were students of Classes XI and XII at Winners Academy, a private coaching institute in Alandi, Pune district.Police personnel and local authorities remained at the site to complete the necessary legal and administrative proceedings.Ministers' express condolences"Deeply saddened by the tragic loss of young lives in the drowning incident at Diveagar Beach in Raigad district, Maharashtra. articles.title: Western militaries are undermining Ukraine’s defence, experts say
articles.summary: A combination of rigid Western military attitudes and Kyiv’s regulatory paralysis leaves fewer weapons at the front.
articles.body:
Mundane regulatory problems in Kyiv and unimaginative institutional thinking in Europe’s militaries are holding up joint weapons production. And that is undermining Ukraine’s battlefield performance and leaving Europe’s armed forces unprepared for modern warfare.

Those are the conclusions of a new report from the Kyiv School of Economics and experts who spoke to Al Jazeera.

For two years, Kyiv has sought to scale up its weapons production by inviting Western partners to fund new production facilities in exchange for battlefield testing. Kyiv receives weapons, Western partners receive know-how.

That formula has led to at least 180 business-to-business partnerships between Ukrainian and foreign partners, but 22 percent of them are stalled, according to the report, Beyond Aid: Making Ukraine Defence Cooperation Work.

One of those stalled ventures is an artillery shell factory that German defence giant Rheinmetall announced a year ago, which should now be starting production. Yet ground has not been broken on the project, because Ukrainian authorities have delayed permits and the government then moved the factory’s site.

There are other legal and bureaucratic problems.

“The process of registering intellectual property is lengthy,” Chris Pool, a visiting fellow at the Centre for Statecraft and National Security (CSNS) at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera. “Iteration cycles move so quickly, often what’s registered and protected is obsolete.”

Former CIA Director General David Petraeus recently discussed how Ukrainian drone manufacturers “can make software changes once a week as required by what the Russians are doing to counter their systems. They can make hardware changes every three or four weeks.”

That is a dizzying speed of innovation by the West’s peacetime standards.

“What happens If the product ends up with a Ukrainian brigade and that brigade then modifies it and adapts it to new developments? Who then owns the intellectual property in the improved product? Does the Ukrainian state have a stake at that point?” said Pool.

“While focusing exclusively on the Ukrainian market may be viable at the initial stage, the absence of a clear export mechanism may later constrain companies’ ability to … integrate Ukrainian-based facilities into wider international supply chains,” said the report.

The problems sometimes lie in Europe’s rigid approach to land warfare, said Pool, who has spoken to Ukrainian teams looking for Western partners.

In 2022, both Russia and Ukraine were fighting exclusively with classic battlefield artillery and heavy armour. Ukraine defeated Russia’s initial attacks with effective use of defensive weapons.

But when Ukraine went on the counteroffensive in 2023, it was unable to compete with Russian scale and production capacity, and quickly adapted.

It designed cheap, long-range drones and missiles to stanch the flow of Russian weapons and fuel to the front, and to destroy Russian refining capacity. It also began to design and build its own first-person view (FPV) drones as a form of artillery.

Ukraine reportedly invested $1bn in drone warfare in 2023, 10 times what it spent in 2022. A New York Times video analysis found that it struck as many Russian armoured vehicles in three months of that year as in all of 2022.

In 2024, Ukraine produced a million FPV drones. In 2025, the production was more than 3 million. This year, Ukraine will produce an estimated 8 million – 16 for every 10 that Russia fields – achieving localised air superiority.

The new weapons came with new tactics and new command structures.

“The most important thing is decentralised command. Ukraine has implemented this more than anyone else,” said Konstantinos Grivas, who teaches advanced weapons systems at the Hellenic Military Academy.

“Units don’t wait for commands from upstairs. They harvest their own information and make their own decisions … You need very capable junior commanders,” he told Al Jazeera.

That dispersed command runs counter to classic military hierarchies and tactics.

“In the UK, there’s a certain amount of arrogance that the British army wouldn’t fight like this, and this is all very interesting, but ultimately, not relevant to us,” said Pool. The Ukrainian teams he spoke to were told, ‘Couldn’t you just partner with [defence companies British Aerospace] or Babcock and then we can deal with the faces with whom we’re used to dealing’,” he said.

Ukraine has demonstrated the challenges of this approach.

In wargames dubbed Combined Resolve in August, Ukrainian drone operators destroyed a US tank brigade by simulating their tactic of dropping armour-piercing artillery directly onto tanks. They did the same to a British brigade in February.

“Faced with teams who are presenting a new technology or navigation that doesn’t rely on GPS, for example, there isn’t that curiosity to find out what’s going on and how this could be adapted to the British Army,” said Pool.

Western militaries have “not even started to shift all of the land forces units into drone infantry,” said Oleksandr Danylyuk, a former senior adviser to Ukraine’s Ministries of Defence and Foreign Affairs, now a land warfare expert at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a London-based think tank.

“If you actually don’t use drones as the main weapon of your infantry, they are obsolete,” he told Al Jazeera. “These people, you recruited and trained to fight with assault rifles, they will never see the enemy. They will be all killed with drones.”

Perhaps the biggest problem of all is money.

The US stopped funding Ukraine last year, and far-right leaders in France and Germany want to follow suit. The European Union is providing the bulk of Ukraine’s military and financial aid for now, but Kyiv overspent in the first half of this year to finance two counteroffensives that took back at least 870sq km of land Russia had occupied, and is impatient for more funds.

Those funds, too, are tied up in European regulations, and Ukrainians feel that with current political trends, receiving them over the long term is an increasingly precarious proposition.

“I don’t see any real chance for any positive transformations in the West,” said Danylyuk.

“Instead of actually using this miracle, which was given by God to the West, and using this Ukrainian heroism and this readiness to sacrifice themselves and the nation, it was just wasted.”

articles.title: The most expensive diesel and petrol prices in the West
articles.summary: Both petrol and diesel prices have risen by a third or more in just the past seven months.
articles.body:
Businesses and charities are being hit by spiralling fuel prices caused by the Iran war.

Last week, diesel prices reached an all-time high and are now about £2 a litre after rising more than 40% since the end of February, with petrol prices climbing nearly 34% in that period.

BBC analysis has identified the most expensive fuel stations across the West, as prices vary across more urban and rural areas.

Alex Wood, from charity Freewheelers which delivers medical supplies, said it has had to dip into reserves to keep afloat. Somerset-based Berry's Coaches has called on the government to freeze fuel duty next year after their fuel costs increased by half since the Middle East conflict began.

Petrol prices have increased by 8% to 174.8p per litre in the past month, while diesel has risen by 9% to 200.1p per litre.

But in the seven months since the US-Israel conflict with Iran erupted, the jump is even bigger - a nearly 34% increase for petrol and more than 40% for diesel.

In real terms, this is an extra 42.5p per litre of petrol and 59p per litre of diesel.

There is variation between different stations in the West too - sometimes as much as 11p per litre for petrol - even if you discount motorway service stations that typically charge a premium.

Alex Wood from the Yeovil branch of Freewheelers, which delivers blood samples and other medical supplies by motorbike, said the impact has been "huge".

"This year since January, it's gone up 20% so it's quite a big increase across our operational costs. It's so unpredictable too."

The charity is now having to dip into its reserves to keep afloat.

"We're having to do a lot more fundraising so that we can keep operating," Wood said.

"We just have to keep going as best we can, we have to keep plodding on."

A taxi company based in Stroud in Gloucestershire previously told the BBC the current situation was a "complete nightmare" as it faced "continual pressure to lowball" its prices to stay afloat.

Berry's Coaches, which runs five services from the South West to London every day, said its costs have risen by £750,000 this year due to climbing fuel prices.

James Berry said it has had "a big impact", but he was confident the company could "weather the storm" as it had done before in its 100-year history.

"We've absorbed a lot of that cost ourselves but unfortunately we've had to apply fuel surcharges across a number of our services - a £2 surcharge on each leg of the journey to London," he said.

"The government have delayed the rise in fuel duty but relatively that's quite a small impact - it will go up by 5p at some point by 2027.

"Really what we would like to see if further fuel duty cuts. That would be a huge benefit from the industry."

Chancellor John Healey said he was "very conscious" of people being hit by spiralling fuel prices caused by international factors.

He said he was "glad" to have frozen fuel duty until the end of the year and brought 'fuel finder' apps to help people find the cheapest petrol stations.

"I'm very aware as I prepare the budget - I'll deliver it a month today - that this needs to be a breathing space budget, recognising the cost of living and the cost of business pressures," he said at the Labour Party Conference.

The BBC has found the most expensive petrol stations by doing an analysis of local prices using Fuel Finder UK , which presents prices from individual stations that are fed into a government dataset.

Excluding petrol stations at motorway services or right next to motorway junctions, which are often much more expensive than average, there is still some variation from place to place.

Some towns like Clevedon, Portishead and Weston-super-Mare are consistently more expensive than other towns and cities in the region.

articles.title: Fires break out at French schools as students protest nationwide
articles.summary: The French government holds a crisis meeting as demonstrations grow and become violent in places.
articles.body:
Fires have broken out at several schools in France, as students protest by blockading education institutions nationwide over school funding and studying conditions.

Blazes were reported at two high schools in Nantes, western France, while another was filmed engulfing the entrance of a school in the northern city of Rouen.

Students are protesting about a lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. University students joined the demonstrations on Thursday, citing similar demands.

The interior ministry said 1,949 people had been arrested on Thursday, with 305 police officers injured. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu held a crisis meeting on Thursday to discuss the unrest.

The government said afterwards that the student-led demonstrations had descended into "urban violence".

Both fires in Nantes spread after a bin was set alight. The blaze at the Nelson Mandela high school, in the city centre, then spread to the front of the building, damaging the entrance hall.

In the southern city of Marseille, staff at Victor Hugo high school were splashed with petrol as protesters reportedly filled containers.

While in the north, a headteacher at Degrugillier high school, in the village of Auchel, was injured in the ear by a wayward firework.

The blockades and protests at French lycées - for 15-18 year olds and equivalent to sixth forms in the UK or high schools in the US - began last week before spreading to hundreds of schools across the country.

So far, 1,027 lycees have been affected by demonstrations, with blockades at 222 of them, according to the interior ministry.

At least 30 universities have also reportedly been blockaded, including campuses in Rennes and Paris.

On Thursday, public transport services in Marseille and Strasbourg were halted due vandalism, threats of violence and to hinder protesters from moving around.

Seventeen-year-old Raphael took part in protests outside a school in Strasbourg, where barriers were used to obstruct nearby tram tracks.

He voiced his frustration at his school's facilities in an interview with news agency AFP, saying some rooms had leaks and that there were not enough toilets.

"The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There's zero budget, zero resources, not enough supervisors," Raphael said.

While France's next general election is still months away, the protests and how French authorities are responding to them has been heavily politicised.

The government and hard-right politicians have blamed the hard left for igniting protests, which are being organised by a union representing lycée students.

Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of a Parisian suburb and member of the radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party defended earlier remarks in which he said violence could be legitimate in some cases - referencing cases in which protesters had allegedly been shot at while not wearing helmets or bulletproof vests.

LFI leader and presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, meanwhile, stressed he was in favour of non-violent protests, while arguing that blaming the left would not solve the issues motivating the demonstrations.

Earlier, leader of the hard-right National Rally Marine Le Pen said: "This is no longer about high school student protests. It is about riots organized by professionals and overseen by deputies from La France Insoumise."

The presidential candidate called for a new anti-rioting law to be passed.

Left-wing mayor of Marseille Benoît Payan condemned the "unacceptable violence" in his city.

While young people were "legitimately concerned" about their future and public services, they must express themselves in a calm fashion, he said.

Eric Ciotti, the Republicans mayor of Nice, said the parents of those found to have damaged school property should be made to pay for the repairs.

articles.title: South Yorkshire Police launches AI tool to reduce 101 calls
articles.summary: South Yorkshire Police says the software will provide advice and answers to non-emergency queries.
articles.body:
A Yorkshire police force has launched a new "AI assistant" on its website in a bid to help reduce the number of 101 calls it receives.

South Yorkshire Police said the Bobbi chatbot could be used for advice and answers about non-emergency incidents. It cannot be used to report a crime or as an alternative to 999.

The technology, which launched on Thursday, has already been rolled out by other forces, including Hampshire & Isle of Wight Constabulary, Thames Valley Police, and Humberside Police.

Ch Supt Cherie Buttle said: "Bobbi will be a useful tool to help reduce calls to 101, save members of the public time, and provide concise and reliable answers to frequently asked questions."

She added: "We receive more than 1,000 101 calls each day and we know that some callers can be waiting 20 minutes or more to speak to our staff during periods of high demand.

"By providing quick responses to non-emergency questions, Bobbi will enable those who prefer to use the AI assistant to save time otherwise spent calling 101 and enable those who do need to speak to one of our call handlers to get through quicker.

"I also recognise some people will have concerns around the use of AI, and I want to emphasise that Bobbi is a secure system. It is an alternative to, not a replacement, for some 101 calls."

The technology will use information provided by South Yorkshire Police to answer queries, rather than other AI assistant tools which work by scouring the internet.

In August the force launched a call handling system using AI software to triage calls to its non-emergency 101 number.

The system was aimed at cutting waiting times for people trying to report crimes by weeding out misdirected, nuisance and prank calls.

articles.title: Death penalty bill for forest arsonists clears Algeria lower house
articles.summary: Human rights organisations accused Algiers of using the law to target political opposition groups.
articles.body:
The Algerian lower house has adopted a law that would allow the death penalty for those convicted of arson, after deadly wildfires have swept through the country’s forests.

Members of the National People’s Assembly (APN) in parliament voted Thursday to amend the country’s penal code to allow the punishment for “anyone who attempts to undermine public security and order, national unity or economic and environmental stability”, according to Algerian media.

President Abdelmadjid Tebboune called for the amendment in September, after at least 12 people died in wildfires in Algeria’s northeast.

The North African country has upheld a long-term moratorium on capital punishment since the last case in 1993.

Human rights organisations, however, urged Parliament not to adopt the law in September and accused the government of using the code as an excuse to employ capital punishment against political opposition groups.

Amnesty International called the move “a deeply retrograde response”, adding that authorities should instead “focus on protecting lives, strengthening prevention and emergency response” in the face of recurring wildfires.

A coalition of other human rights groups signed a letter calling on authorities to halt any changes to the penal code and suggested that the death penalty has “never deterred arsonists from committing their crimes”.

They agreed that perpetrators must be held to account and provide restitution for the damage and loss of life.

During deadly wildfires in 2021 , Algeria detained at least 30 people, including seven members of the Movement for the Self-Determination of Kabylie ( MAK ), which authorities declared a “ terrorist organisation”.

Justice Minister Lotfi Boudjemaa defended the recent change and said, “The adoption of the death penalty for these acts is the appropriate legal response to curb these crimes.”

Despite the moratorium, death sentences have been handed out before, including in “terror-related” cases. Tebboune said that those death sentences would be enacted once their appeals were exhausted.

The law is now set to be reviewed by the upper house, the Council of the Nation, before being officially ratified by Tebboune.

articles.title: UK in talks with EU partners to release strategic fuel reserves if needed, BBC understands
articles.summary: President Donald Trump has threatened to ban diesel exports in a bid to ease prices in the US.
articles.body:
Britain is in talks with EU partners to release additional strategic fuel reserves, including diesel, if needed, the BBC understands.

The talks come after President Donald Trump threatened to ban diesel exports from the US in a bid to reduce record prices at the pumps for Americans.

Diesel prices in the UK also hit record highs this week and are hovering just under 200p per litre, according to motoring organisation the RAC.

The US is a vital supplier of diesel to the world, exporting between 1.2 and 1.5 million barrels per day, with experts warning a ban on shipments abroad could put further pressure on prices in other countries.

"We're thinking about it very seriously," Trump said of an export ban at the weekend.

Energy Minister Martin McCluskey was on a call with European counterparts on Thursday to discuss the potential ban.

A source familiar with the discussions told the BBC it was prudent to prepare a co-ordinated response with other countries, including those across EU, but added that there were still European reserves left from a coordinated release of strategic fuel stocks earlier in the year.

"We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry," a government spokesperson said. The government has stressed that there is no cause for concern about potential diesel shortages, though prices are expected to rise further.

What a US diesel export ban could mean for you

A European Commission spokesperson said today that there were "lots of calls, lots of meetings" taking place on the diesel situation, including with "high level contacts" in the US administration.

A meeting of the governing board of the International Energy Agency (IEA) is taking place tomorrow.

Prices of petrol and diesel globally have skyrocketed since the outbreak of the US-Israel war in Iran in February. The closure of the vital Strait of Hormuz, which typically transports around a fifth of the world's oil and gas, has pushed up the price of products made from oil.

An export ban from Russia, also a major supplier of diesel, has added to the pressure on prices.

Trump has argued that keeping any surplus barrels of diesel in the US would lower pump prices domestically, offering immediate relief to drivers, truckers, and businesses ahead of the midterm elections.

But David Fyfe, chief economist at Argus Media, said cutting off American supply would likely cause international prices to skyrocket.

Diesel prices have hit an all-time high in the UK, with the latest RAC figures showing average pump prices at 199.79p per litre, up from 142.38p

Diesel is harder to refine than gasoline and, because it is used by the haulage industry and in agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.

The UK is heavily reliant on imports. Although the four refineries in the UK make more than enough petrol to meet demand, they do not make enough diesel for the country's needs.

There were 15.1 million diesel vehicles on UK roads at the end of June, according to the Department for Transport. That is a drop from 15.7 million a year before.

There were 9.8 million diesel cars, down year on year from 10.4 million.

articles.title: Europe’s drone defences have a Moldova-sized gap. Can Washington plug it?
articles.summary: A recent drone explosion near Chișinău highlights Moldova’s critical vulnerabilities regarding airspace monitoring and emergency alert systems amid a sharp increase in unauthorized flights.
articles.body:
As most of Moldova slept, around 4.20 a.m. on Sept. 18, residents on the eastern periphery of Chișinău, the capital, reported a bright flash and a sizable explosion. Police searched for hours to determine the cause before finding the remnants of a drone , including a jet engine, scattered across a harvested field near the village of Colonița. The village lies roughly seven kilometers east of the capital and forms part of the Chișinău municipality. The blast was heard in parts of the capital. Strikingly, Moldova’s Ministry of Defense said it had recorded no unauthorized overflight that night .

Moldova sits between Ukraine and Romania. It is an EU candidate but remains outside of NATO. It possesses limited radar coverage and no national mobile phone alert system in operation. This is a problem, given that Moldova has lived with falling drones and fragments since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

However, the geography of the Colonița explosion and the increasing frequency of drone incursions in Moldovan airspace reveal a serious vulnerability for the nation.

The explosion of Sept. 18 is the first known case of a drone falling and exploding within the Chișinău municipality. Granted, previous drones had flown over the capital before, but this one came down within its jurisdiction. Residents reported the explosion before the authorities could identify its location. When a drone explodes so close to the country’s political, economic and populational center, the first warning should not be the sound of its impact.

Moldovan authorities recorded four unauthorized airspace incidents in 2022, six in 2023, ten in 2024, and 17 in 2025. By Aug. 19, 2026, however, Moldova had already counted 16; by Sept. 24? An alarming 44 violations . Four aerial objects crossed Moldovan airspace on the morning of Sept. 24 alone , prompting the temporary closure of northern airspace.

Twenty-nine additional violations in six weeks require more than stock platitudes about the consequences of a war next door. Such violations indicate a sharply accelerating exposure of Moldovan territory, right up to the capital’s edge. The precise reason for each crossing remains uncertain. Moldova need not establish a drone’s intended destination before improving detection and public warning.

President Maia Sandu has acknowledged that surveillance is improving but remains insufficient, and that existing missiles, anti-aircraft weaponry and electronic systems protect only selected critical infrastructure. The EU committed, this July, €120 million towards a medium-range air-defense system for Moldova, which will take time to acquire and deploy. But these investments are of immeasurable importance. So is the closing of the warning gap before they come into service. Chișinău should agree to a faster, routine exchange of flight tracks and alerts with Romania and Ukraine.

This is not an abstract failing. When the same drone that later crashed near Mihăilenii Vechi first crossed into Romanian airspace on Sept. 8 , RO-Alert, Romania’s national alert system, reached phones across five Romanian counties within minutes. No comparable message reached anyone in Moldova’s Rîșcani district, where the drone came down later. Norway’s prime minister later said a drone had nearly struck Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s aircraft as it departed Chișinău. Moldova’s own ambassador in Washington said the timing was probably “not an accident.”

Moldova’s own early alert system equivalent, MD-ALERT , exists for now only as an approved concept. Greenlit in March, it is financed by a World Bank loan and is due to become operational in 2027. Even then, it is built around floods and heatwaves, not falling drones; nothing currently ties it to the radar and interception systems the EU’s money is meant to fund.

Washington has a stake here too. Between February 2022 and September 2024, the U.S. announced up to $1 billion in assistance to Moldova . That commitment hasn’t disappeared: In May, Washington announced $8 million over four years to strengthen Moldova’s cybersecurity and harden its government systems against attack. It is a sign the U.S. still sees Moldova’s resilience as worth backing. But that support has stayed on the cyber side. Nothing comparable has followed for drones, radar or public warning, even as airspace violations have more than doubled since last year.

None of this requires a new aid package, or even a new argument. A modest counter-drone allocation through Foreign Military Financing or the U.S. contribution to NATO’s Defence and Related Security Capacity Building initiative would extend Washington’s existing support to the threat now most directly facing Moldova.

The Colonița event was fortunate only in where the drone happened to land, not in how quickly anyone learned it had. A standing, real-time arrangement to share flight-track data with Bucharest and Kyiv costs little beyond political will. A narrow, security-specific alert for the handful of areas at risk, including Chișinău and near the Ukrainian border, could be running well before the broader civil protection system it will eventually sit alongside. Romania’s alerts on Sept. 8 concerned a different drone, ten days before the Colonița explosion. They show what a timely warning can look like.

Until Moldova can give its own residents similar notice, the next drone may again announce itself before the state does.

Will Kingston-Cox is founder and managing director of Europinion. Laurențiu Pleșca is a program officer at the German Marshall Fund of the United States.

articles.title: Dual U.K.-Iranian national arrested over security incident at U.S.-run air base in England
articles.summary: LONDON — Police on Thursday arrested a dual U.K.-Iranian national on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at a U.S.-run military air base in England that British authorities have linked to Tehran.
articles.body: LONDON — Police on Thursday arrested a dual U.K.-Iranian national on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at a U.S.-run military air base in England that British authorities have linked to Tehran. The 27-year-old man was arrested in London on Thursday, and police have searched two properties in the U.K. capital, Counter Terrorism Policing said in a statement. A 26-year-old British national was interviewed by police “under caution,” which means the interview was recorded and can be used in future prosecutions. On Sunday, five men, all British nationals in their 20s and from London, were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terror offenses close to the RAF Fairford air base, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran. The suspects have since been released on bail. Police say they found a quantity of an accelerant - gasoline - in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives. Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counter terrorism policing, said the investigation “is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of inquiry. “As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles — including possible foreign state involvement,” she said. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the U.K. sees “strong indications” that Iran played a part in the incident. Iran denies involvement. The base 100 miles west of London has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including this year’s war with Iran. Top U.S. officials have criticized the decision to grant five suspects bail, with President Donald Trump saying “I wouldn’t have done that” and Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying a lot of people were “disturbed” by the move. Burnham said authorities have the investigation under “the strongest grip and the closest control,” and British officials had been “talking to counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done.” U.K. officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arsons and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue.

articles.title: Treasury targets Iranian auto, rail sectors in latest round of sanctions
articles.summary: The Treasury Department sanctioned Iranian auto and rail industries on Thursday, the latest salvo in its economic campaign against the Islamic Republic. The Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned the entirety of those industries — going after automobile, train and manufacturing companies — which the administration views as critical sources of funding for…
articles.body:
The Treasury Department sanctioned Iranian auto and rail industries on Thursday, the latest salvo in its economic campaign against the Islamic Republic.

The Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned the entirety of those industries — going after automobile, train and manufacturing companies — which the administration views as critical sources of funding for the regime, the department noted in a release .

The OFAC’s actions are part of a broader crackdown on Iranian transportation. Last month, the Treasury sanctioned all of Iran’s airlines .

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Thursday his department’s financial warfare campaign against Iran — which he dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast” — has “severely diminished” the regime’s “ability to fund its war machine and inflict terror” via its own military, as well as through regional proxies.

“Today’s action directly targets Iran’s enablers and lays the groundwork for the United States and our partners to drain the regime’s revenue once and for all,” Bessent said in the release.

The Iranian auto sector, the Treasury noted, is an “essential component” of the country’s defense industrial base.

Iran’s domestic auto industry is dominated by two firms, Iran Khodro Company and SAIPA Iranian Automobile Manufacturing Company, which control more than 90 percent of the market.

The Treasury honed on in Iran Khodro Diesel and SAIPA, along with two of its subsidiaries, for its latest sanctions. The companies manufacture buses, trucks and diesel engines, passenger cars, commercial cars and motorcycles.

As for the Iranian rail sector, which the administration says the regime has used to transport oil amid the American naval blockade of its ports, the Treasury is targeting two state-owned firms: Islamic Republic of Iran Railway Company and the Raja Passenger Trains Company.

Bessent has targeted a swath of Iranian industries as part of his economic campaign , urging other countries to cut off ties to Tehran to avoid the U.S. cutting them off from its dollar system.

The U.S. military campaign against Iran, which hit the seven-month mark this week, has marched on into October after President Trump rejected a short-term ceasefire proposal from Iranian officials.

The latest Treasury actions also crack down on foreign companies supplying auto and truck parts to the Middle Eastern country.

Those firms include the United Arab Emirates (UAE)-based Integrated Auto Parts and the Turkey-based Troy Trading Arac Parcalari Sanayi Ve Ticaret.

While the administration has worked with European allies on choking Iran economically, it has also sought assistance from Gulf states — including the UAE.
